activities.title: Light and sound: two kinds of wave

differentiation.support: Provide the student notes open at the wavelength definition so learners can follow how speed divided by frequency gives the wavelength before they try the worksheet calculation.

activities.title: The wave equation: v = f x wavelength
Here is the trap, sprung on purpose
Waves carry energy, particles vibrate in place

differentiation.stretch: Ask learners to explain why the flash arrives before the thunder using both speeds before they take the exit ticket.

activities.title: Flash first: light far outruns sound

assessmentPoints: Wave-kind answers in the opening activity
Trap answers in the third activity and the closing exit ticket
successCriteria: I can say light is transverse and sound is longitudinal, with the particle vibration across the direction of travel for light and along it for sound
I can explain that we see lightning before we hear thunder because light travels at about 300,000,000 metres per second while sound manages only 340
objectives.text: Tell transverse and longitudinal waves apart and give light and sound as the examples

assessmentPoints: Vocabulary answers in the fourth activity
Definition answers in the closing worksheet
successCriteria: I can define frequency as how many full waves pass a point each second, measured in hertz
I can define wavelength as the length of one full wave, from one crest to the next, measured in metres
objectives.text: Define the key vocabulary of waves: wave, transverse wave, longitudinal wave, frequency and wavelength

assessmentPoints: Wavelength answers in the second activity
Speed answers in the closing worksheet
successCriteria: I can rearrange v = f x wavelength to wavelength = v / f, such as 340 divided by 170 giving 2 metres
I can calculate a wave speed from frequency times wavelength, such as 5 hertz times 3 metres giving 15 metres per second
objectives.text: Use the wave equation v = f x wavelength to find a speed, a frequency or a wavelength
